scope.negative_control: The punctuation case is deliberately Java-invalid and excluded from scoring; it verifies that the new boundary does not silently retain a legal prefix from an illegal complete code.

implementation_audit.java_provenance: CommandFactoryNote uses [%pLN_.]+ for both forms, then passes the captured code through diagram.cleanId before quark resolution; EntityImageNote emits the resulting quark qualified name. Its multiline regex permits optional tags, stereotype, and color after CODE.
implementation_audit.rust_provenance: crates/rustuml-parser/src/parse/component.rs:34 defines the shared code token; lines 333-343 use it for both forms. The multiline regex admits only an optional color after the code, unlike Java's optional stereotype path. Lines 711 and 776 store the raw capture without the Java-observed Unicode identity projection.
implementation_audit.anti_overfit: The diff adds a general Unicode regex token and no fixture-dependent branch, golden read, baseline/comparator edit, post-hoc SVG surgery, or unexplained parity constant. The failures are model omissions, not evidence of fixture shaping.

findings.title: Valid multiline note stereotypes erase the named note
findings.impact: A Java-valid Component note with a legal dotted code has no Rust AST note or SVG entity, so the claimed shared command grammar is incomplete.

findings.title: Unicode named-note identity does not match Java's shipped SVG
findings.impact: Rust preserves raw Unicode in data-qualified-name while Java's rendered names are OuterUnicodeB.M.trique..elta_7 and R.sum...elta_9. The account's claim that the captured token proceeds unchanged is false for the product output.

residue: The dotted later-relation endpoint remains unsupported in Component rendering, exactly as declared in the account; the valid residue input is preserved.
Detailed note color/stereotype styling is outside the claimed identity mechanism, but legal modifier recognition is not: without it, the named note disappears.
conclusion: REJECTED. The dot-boundary repair works for ordinary ASCII codes, but it does not model the complete valid command suffix grammar or Java's observable Unicode identity projection.
